items.title: org.bouncycastle:bctls-klog-jdk18on 1.86.1 发布, The Bouncy Castle Java APIs for the TLS, including a JSSE provider, built as the RFC 9850 key logging variant. Unlike the standard bctls jar, this jar is able to disclose the secrets of the TLS connections it makes, reporting them to a TlsKeyLog implementation named by the org.bouncycastle.tls.keylog.class security property, and disclosing nothing if that property is unset. Its JSSE provider info string is also marked as a key logger so that a running JVM can report which of the two jars it was given. It is a drop-in replacement for bctls-jdk18on rather than an addition to it, and the two must not be placed on the same classpath. It is intended for diagnostics and interoperability testing, not for production use. The APIs are designed primarily to be used in conjunction with the BC Java provider but may also be used with other providers providing cryptographic services. This jar is designed to best work with Java 1.8 and later.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:homing-rel-grid 0.1.0 发布, The Relation Grid (RFC 0050 · Episode 2), as its own project. A grid
        that captures intents and ARRANGES cells, and holds no value: a
        relation is identities, columns and a cell manager, the domain owns
        every cell for its whole life, and edit, commit and update are the
        domain's operations that never change an arrangement.

        rel-channel is the ask channel's core — a notification handed over, a
        question waited on behind the mask — the family's, under a surface.
        rel-grid-protocol is the ask protocol: every question and answer
        declared once as a Java record, its JS class generated at build time.

        rel-grid-selection is the selection: an ordered list of ranges over
        positions, in a module that imports nothing at all.

        rel-grid is the primitive — plain JS classes with no runtime
        dependency on anything, packaged as homing DomModules for this stack.
        rel-tree is the tree view (Episode 3): the second component on the
        same doctrine, over the channel and the protocol and nothing of the grid.
        json-kit is the first out-of-the-box offering: a JSON viewer on the tree
        view — domain-side code that ships, holding values as any domain does.
        rel-grid-workbench is the solo studio of benches that try to make it
        fail, on the workspace shell.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:rel-grid-protocol 0.1.0 发布, The Relation Grid's ask protocol (RFC 0050 · Episode 2, ext4 and ext5).
        Every question the grid asks and every answer it accepts is declared
        ONCE, as a Java record, and its JS class is GENERATED from that record
        at build time. Nothing about a payload's shape is written twice.

        Per the Generated and Hand-Written Live Apart doctrine this module's
        src/main/resources is empty: the served JS is produced by
        RelGridProtocolGen.main() into target/classes during process-classes,
        under the filename the DomModule's simple name requires.

        Data only — no DOM, no grid. Domain code depends on this to answer
        without depending on the grid, which is ext4's law 202.

        Round one carries the first kind: a selection notification, which
        expects no answer. Codecs are not generated, because nothing serialises
        one yet (law 214).

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:rel-tree 0.1.0 发布, The Tree View (RFC 0050 · Episode 3-ext1): the second component on
        Episode 2's doctrine, and not a grid. A tree relation answers PLACES
        — the tree structure, { key, depth, fold } in pre-order, the binding
        contract — and manages CELLS, the domain's, one per node, opaque to
        the tree. The tree owns the rows, the indent, the caret, the cursor
        and the keys; fold and unfold are regular questions on the ask
        channel, answered with the whole View to present or nothing, so a
        tree is lazy by default and a domain bounds a large one by what it
        answers. Rows are positions, grown at the tail.

        Depends on rel-channel for the channel's core and on the family's
        protocol crate for its messages, and on nothing of the grid's table.
        The JS has no runtime dependency on homing; the Java side is packaging.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:rel-grid-group 0.1.0 发布, The Relation Grid GROUP (RFC 0050 · Episode 2, the federation re-read):
        an ordered list of tables, each an ordinary RelGrid that does not know
        it is in one, stacked down one column of boxes with a FENCE between
        every two and around the ends — a slot the group mints and the domain
        fills. Members are identities; the group's own state is which show, in
        what order, and (later) which are folded. Everything inside a member —
        its cursor, its selection, its copy, its handover, the domain its ask
        reaches — is the member's own and untouched.

        What the group shares is the one thing separate tables cannot agree
        on by themselves: column geometry. It is the single writer of widths
        — it hears any member's resize report, applies it to the siblings
        through their public verbs, and reports once — and it reaches into no
        member's layout to do it.

        A module of its own because the guarantee is structural: this module
        depends on the grid, and the grid's does not depend on this one. Not
        one line of group code lives in the table.

        on by themselves: column geometry. It is the single writer of widths
        — it hears any member's resize report, applies it to the siblings
        through their public verbs, and reports once — and it reaches into no
        member's layout to do it.

        A module of its own because the guarantee is structural: this module
        depends on the grid, and the grid's does not depend on this one. Not
        one line of group code lives in the table.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:rel-grid-selection 0.1.0 发布, The Relation Grid's selection (RFC 0050 · Episode 2, map 5), and
        nothing else. A selection is an ORDERED LIST OF RANGES, each a
        rectangle of positions owning both its corners, the smallest 1x1,
        never merged and never reordered. The module manages that list and
        answers what is selected when something else is triggered; it never
        initiates anything.

        A module of its own because the guarantee is worth making structural:
        this one imports NOTHING. Not the view maps, not the layout, not the
        cells, not the cursor — the two operations that need any of those take
        them as arguments (the cursor's position for the implicit 1x1, the
        extents for select-all). No DOM. Positions in, positions out, which is
        why its whole test suite runs on a bare JS context with no stub.

        What is deliberately NOT here: the cursor, which is identity-first,
        tells its cell and paints, so it stays with the grid; clamping, which
        belongs to whoever knows the presented space; and the paint, which is
        the layout's. See map 5 laws 215-218.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:rel-grid 0.1.0 发布, The Relation Grid primitive (RFC 0050 · Episode 2). The root principle
        is the whole contract: the grid captures intents and arranges cells;
        it holds, fetches, pushes and writes NO VALUE. A relation is
        identities, columns and a CELL MANAGER (cellFor) — the grid asks for a
        cell once per identity and places it; the domain owns the cell for its
        whole life and updates it directly.

        What is here: arrangement over an immutable root relation; a cursor
        that is an identity with a position as its fallback; the shallow/deep
        discipline (single click and arrows are the grid's; Enter or a
        double-click hands the cell control until it releases); column widths
        held by identity, applied by position, in place. What is not: sort,
        filter, selection ranges — the relation's and later rounds'.

        Value-freedom is enforced mechanically — a test scans every grid
        module for the value verbs and fails the build on the first one. The
        JS has no runtime dependency on homing; the Java side is packaging.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:json-kit 0.1.0 发布, The JSON kit: an out-of-the-box JSON viewer on the tree view (RFC 0050
        · Episode 3). DOMAIN-SIDE code that ships, as the stock cells do: a
        JSON value is exactly what a relation holds and a tree never sees — a
        relation that answers a value's PLACES, object members and array
        elements by JSON-pointer key, lazily under the fold; a cell per node
        that draws the key and the value in the theme's colour; and a viewer
        that composes the two over a RelTree for a host that wants one line.
        The tree is not changed for it, and could not be: the kit is a consumer
        of rel-tree, one crate over, holding values as any domain does.

        Depends on rel-tree, and through it on the channel's core and the
        family's protocol.

io.github.captainssingapura-hue.homing.ssjs:rel-channel 0.1.0 发布, The ask channel's CORE (RFC 0050 · Episode 2, ext4 and ext6; Episode
        3-ext1), the family's and not the grid's: one function the host gave, a
        NOTIFICATION handed over and never waited on, a QUESTION waited on
        with the person stopped — the mask session with its delay and its
        hold, the panel handle, one question at a time — and nothing else.
        What is asked and what is answered are the customers' business: the
        grid's channel keeps its selection, copy and view handover over this
        core, and the tree's keeps its fold and unfold.

        The SURFACE is what the mask needs of a presentation — openMask,
        closeMask, setMasked, openPanel, closePanel, focus — six functions a
        layout has. No DOM is touched here but through them; no payload is
        read. A crate of its own so that both presentations reach it without
        either reaching the other.

        files (file presence is the opt-in signal the processor honours), `doctor`
        reports the project's VibeTags health — build-tool wiring, active platforms,
        marker integrity. Run it without installing anything:

            jbang se.deversity.vibetags:vibetags-cli:1.3.5 init --list

        The platform list and marker rules are read from vibetags-processor, so this
        tool cannot drift from what the processor actually does.

        a coherent vibetags-annotations + vibetags-processor pair without specifying
        each version individually.

        Recommended setup — annotations on the compile classpath, processor on the
        annotation-processor path only (the processor jar pulls in slf4j/logback,
        which has no business on consumer code's compileClasspath):

        Maven:
            <dependencyManagement>
                <dependencies>
                    <dependency>
                        <groupId>se.deversity.vibetags</groupId>
                        <artifactId>vibetags-bom</artifactId>
                        <version>1.3.0</version>
                        <type>pom</type>
                        <scope>import</scope>
                    </dependency>
                </dependencies>
            </dependencyManagement>

        Gradle:
            implementation platform('se.deversity.vibetags:vibetags-bom:1.3.5')
            annotationProcessor platform('se.deversity.vibetags:vibetags-bom:1.3.5')
            compileOnly 'se.deversity.vibetags:vibetags-annotations'
            annotationProcessor 'se.deversity.vibetags:vibetags-processor'
